1debf1b418bc.reason: DDL issued from a console command or service rather than a migration: temporary tables built to stage a bulk computation (UpdateAIImageUsageCounts, WhatJobs, AuthorityStats) and the online-schema steps in MigrateReachBoundsSchemaCommand. c4573eab864d.goldenSql: (JSON_EXTRACT(settings, '$.browseMaxMinutes') IS NOT NULL OR JSON_EXTRACT(settings, '$.browseMaxDistance') IS NOT NULL)
c4573eab864d.reason: MySQL JSON accessors inside an otherwise-ORM chain. Laravel does have a JSON where syntax (->where('settings->key', 1)), but it does NOT emit the same SQL: it wraps the extraction in json_unquote() and casts, so a predicate written as JSON_EXTRACT(settings, '$.k') = 1 changes meaning at the edges - notably for JSON true/false versus 1/0, and for a key that is absent rather than null, both of which appear in these very predicates (several read `= true`, several test IS NULL). Converting them would be a behaviour change dressed as a refactor, on settings that gate who gets mailed. They stay raw until someone ports them deliberately, with data to check against.
c4573eab864d.porting: PostgreSQL: this is the single biggest dialect gap in this manifest. JSON_EXTRACT becomes -> / ->> and JSON_UNQUOTE disappears into ->>, but the NULL and boolean semantics differ again, so every one of these needs reading rather than substituting. Doing it behind a helper (one place that renders a settings predicate) is worth more than converting them in situ first.

c65bfcd41aa8.reason: An aggregate given an alias inside a SELECT list. Laravel's ->count()/->sum()/->avg()/->min()/->max() are first-class but each computes ONE value and issues its own statement; there is no builder form for 'select these aggregates, aliased, alongside these columns'. The only conversion available is ->select(DB::raw('COUNT(*) AS cnt')), and DB::raw is itself a raw site in this inventory - the site would move from surface fragment to surface expression and nothing would be converted. 00811b58fbbf.goldenSql: UPDATE IGNORE messages_history SET msgid = ? WHERE msgid = ?
00811b58fbbf.reason: UPDATE IGNORE has no query-builder form. Laravel provides insertOrIgnore() for INSERT IGNORE - so the INSERT side of this pattern IS convertible and is not covered by this rule - but there is no updateOrIgnore(), and the modifier is load-bearing here rather than decorative: TnDedupCommand repoints messages_history and messages_postings rows at a surviving message id, and IGNORE is what lets the statement skip the rows that would collide with an existing (msgid, ...) unique key instead of aborting the whole update. Reproducing that in the builder means either pre-filtering the collisions with a second query (a different statement with a race between the two) or catching the integrity error per row. Both are worse than the statement that is there.
00811b58fbbf.porting: PostgreSQL: no IGNORE modifier exists. The equivalent is an explicit predicate excluding the rows that would collide, or ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING where the operation can be expressed as an upsert. This needs a per-statement rewrite with the unique key in mind, not a mechanical substitution.

fe1d3f14e974.reason: MySQL JSON accessors inside an otherwise-ORM chain. Laravel does have a JSON where syntax (->where('settings->key', 1)), but it does NOT emit the same SQL: it wraps the extraction in json_unquote() and casts, so a predicate written as JSON_EXTRACT(settings, '$.k') = 1 changes meaning at the edges - notably for JSON true/false versus 1/0, and for a key that is absent rather than null, both of which appear in these very predicates (several read `= true`, several test IS NULL). Converting them would be a behaviour change dressed as a refactor, on settings that gate who gets mailed. They stay raw until someone ports them deliberately, with data to check against.
fe1d3f14e974.porting: PostgreSQL: this is the single biggest dialect gap in this manifest. JSON_EXTRACT becomes -> / ->> and JSON_UNQUOTE disappears into ->>, but the NULL and boolean semantics differ again, so every one of these needs reading rather than substituting. Doing it behind a helper (one place that renders a settings predicate) is worth more than converting them in situ first.

2145f991b248.reason: A scalar SQL function applied to a column - LEFT(textbody, 500), COALESCE(namefull, nameshort), GREATEST(...), CAST(...) and the like. Same position as the aliased-aggregate rule: the builder can select columns, not expressions over them, so the only conversion available is ->select(DB::raw('LEFT(textbody, 500) as body')) and DB::raw is itself a raw site here - the site moves from one surface to another and nothing is converted. Doing the work in PHP instead is not equivalent: LEFT(textbody, 500) truncates in the database so only 500 bytes cross the wire, and the queries using it are batch jobs over large text columns where that is the point. COALESCE and GREATEST additionally participate in WHERE and ORDER BY, where moving them to PHP is not possible at all.
2145f991b248.porting: PostgreSQL: LEFT/RIGHT/SUBSTRING/CONCAT/COALESCE/GREATEST/LEAST/LOWER/UPPER/TRIM/CAST are standard and port unchanged. IFNULL becomes COALESCE, IF(a,b,c) becomes CASE WHEN a THEN b ELSE c END, and CONCAT_WS exists but treats NULLs differently - those three need rewriting, the rest do not.

fc3cabdc2a63.reason: MySQL spatial functions and the project's own haversine() SQL function. The builder has no spatial vocabulary at all, so these can only ever be raw text; converting means DB::raw, which converts nothing. They are also the statements most likely to be index-sensitive, so rewriting their shape casually risks a table scan on locations.
fc3cabdc2a63.porting: PostgreSQL/PostGIS: ST_Contains/ST_Intersects/ST_Within carry over by name, but SRID axis order differs (MySQL is lat/lng for 4326, PostGIS is lng/lat) and will silently transpose coordinates if unhandled. haversine() is a project-defined MySQL function with no Postgres counterpart - port it as ST_DWithin on geography, which is both correct and index-assisted, rather than translating the arithmetic.

4fc5ec8e010e.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience.
4fc5ec8e010e.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.

55cf330ff372.goldenSql: INSERT INTO users_emails (email, canon, validatekey, backwards, validatetime) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, NOW()) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE validatekey = ?, validatetime = NOW()
55cf330ff372.reason: A write that stores the DATABASE's clock - VALUES (..., NOW()) or SET x = NOW(). The builder can express the statement but not the value: ->update(['x' => DB::raw('NOW()')]) keeps a raw site, and ->update(['x' => now()]) binds a timestamp taken from the PHP process instead. That second form is the one that looks like a clean conversion and is not, because it moves the clock from the database to the application - across a batch host whose time can drift from the cluster's, on columns (validatetime, giftaidclaimed, latestmessage) that later get compared against other database-generated timestamps. The individual case that established this is site 029b3600e99d, GiftAidClaimService's claimed-at stamp, declined for the same reason before this rule existed; the rule generalises that decision rather than inventing it.
55cf330ff372.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() exists with the same transaction-start semantics, so these port unchanged. If a true wall-clock instant is wanted rather than the transaction's, clock_timestamp() is the closer equivalent - a question worth asking per column at porting time, not before.

978be101f754.reason: A statement whose entire select list is NOW() and which reads from no table - MigrateReachBoundsSchemaCommand uses it to stamp the database's clock either side of a long schema step. DB::table() needs a table, and there is none; the builder has no from-less select. Taking the time in PHP instead defeats the purpose, which is specifically to read the DATABASE's clock rather than the application's - the command is comparing timings across a migration that may span replicas.

f326d3d0e074.reason: DDL issued from a console command or service rather than a migration: temporary tables built to stage a bulk computation (UpdateAIImageUsageCounts, WhatJobs, AuthorityStats) and the online-schema steps in MigrateReachBoundsSchemaCommand. Laravel's Schema builder covers permanent schema, not CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE with an explicit column/collation spec, and not ALTER carrying MySQL's ALGORITHM/LOCK hints - which is exactly why these were written as statements. Converting them would mean Schema::connection(...)->statement(...), which is the same raw SQL with more ceremony. The temporary tables in particular are part of an algorithm, not a schema: they exist for the length of one command run.

a30e89fc4716.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience. Recorded separately for the expression surface (DB::raw) because the extractor classifies the two differently, but the construct - and the reason it cannot leave SQL - is identical.
a30e89fc4716.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.

d5a39f2eb53a.reason: An aggregate given an alias inside a SELECT list. Laravel's ->count()/->sum()/->avg()/->min()/->max() are first-class but each computes ONE value and issues its own statement; there is no builder form for 'select these aggregates, aliased, alongside these columns'. The only conversion available is ->select(DB::raw('COUNT(*) AS cnt')), and DB::raw is itself a raw site in this inventory - the site would move from surface fragment to surface expression and nothing would be converted. Splitting one grouped scan into N separate aggregate queries is not equivalent either.
d5a39f2eb53a.porting: PostgreSQL: standard SQL, ports unchanged. GROUP_CONCAT is the exception - it becomes string_agg(expr, delim) with a different argument order, and any ORDER BY inside it moves too.

4cfdde71ba6b.reason: MySQL spatial functions and the project's own haversine() SQL function. The builder has no spatial vocabulary at all, so these can only ever be raw text; converting means DB::raw, which converts nothing. They are also the statements most likely to be index-sensitive, so rewriting their shape casually risks a table scan on locations. Recorded separately for the expression surface (DB::raw) because the extractor classifies the two differently, but the construct - and the reason it cannot leave SQL - is identical.
4cfdde71ba6b.porting: PostgreSQL/PostGIS: ST_Contains/ST_Intersects/ST_Within carry over by name, but SRID axis order differs (MySQL is lat/lng for 4326, PostGIS is lng/lat) and will silently transpose coordinates if unhandled. haversine() is a project-defined MySQL function with no Postgres counterpart - port it as ST_DWithin on geography, which is both correct and index-assisted, rather than translating the arithmetic.

a6d3c0be64c4.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience.
a6d3c0be64c4.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.

b637ecdfe0a5.reason: MySQL JSON accessors inside an otherwise-ORM chain. Laravel does have a JSON where syntax (->where('settings->key', 1)), but it does NOT emit the same SQL: it wraps the extraction in json_unquote() and casts, so a predicate written as JSON_EXTRACT(settings, '$.k') = 1 changes meaning at the edges - notably for JSON true/false versus 1/0, and for a key that is absent rather than null, both of which appear in these very predicates (several read `= true`, several test IS NULL). Converting them would be a behaviour change dressed as a refactor, on settings that gate who gets mailed. They stay raw until someone ports them deliberately, with data to check against.
b637ecdfe0a5.porting: PostgreSQL: this is the single biggest dialect gap in this manifest. JSON_EXTRACT becomes -> / ->> and JSON_UNQUOTE disappears into ->>, but the NULL and boolean semantics differ again, so every one of these needs reading rather than substituting. Doing it behind a helper (one place that renders a settings predicate) is worth more than converting them in situ first.

0cc4478c6b59.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience.
0cc4478c6b59.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.

41c483169a42.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience.
41c483169a42.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.

b271269c7634.reason: A write that stores the DATABASE's clock - VALUES (..., NOW()) or SET x = NOW(). The builder can express the statement but not the value: ->update(['x' => DB::raw('NOW()')]) keeps a raw site, and ->update(['x' => now()]) binds a timestamp taken from the PHP process instead. That second form is the one that looks like a clean conversion and is not, because it moves the clock from the database to the application - across a batch host whose time can drift from the cluster's, on columns (validatetime, giftaidclaimed, latestmessage) that later get compared against other database-generated timestamps. The individual case that established this is site 029b3600e99d, GiftAidClaimService's claimed-at stamp, declined for the same reason before this rule existed; the rule generalises that decision rather than inventing it.
b271269c7634.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() exists with the same transaction-start semantics, so these port unchanged. If a true wall-clock instant is wanted rather than the transaction's, clock_timestamp() is the closer equivalent - a question worth asking per column at porting time, not before.

1b511e34081f.reason: MySQL spatial functions and the project's own haversine() SQL function. The builder has no spatial vocabulary at all, so these can only ever be raw text; converting means DB::raw, which converts nothing. They are also the statements most likely to be index-sensitive, so rewriting their shape casually risks a table scan on locations.
1b511e34081f.porting: PostgreSQL/PostGIS: ST_Contains/ST_Intersects/ST_Within carry over by name, but SRID axis order differs (MySQL is lat/lng for 4326, PostGIS is lng/lat) and will silently transpose coordinates if unhandled. haversine() is a project-defined MySQL function with no Postgres counterpart - port it as ST_DWithin on geography, which is both correct and index-assisted, rather than translating the arithmetic.

ff6e10c4a967.reason: A scalar SQL function applied to a column - LEFT(textbody, 500), COALESCE(namefull, nameshort), GREATEST(...), CAST(...) and the like. Same position as the aliased-aggregate rule: the builder can select columns, not expressions over them, so the only conversion available is ->select(DB::raw('LEFT(textbody, 500) as body')) and DB::raw is itself a raw site here - the site moves from one surface to another and nothing is converted. Doing the work in PHP instead is not equivalent: LEFT(textbody, 500) truncates in the database so only 500 bytes cross the wire, and the queries using it are batch jobs over large text columns where that is the point. COALESCE and GREATEST additionally participate in WHERE and ORDER BY, where moving them to PHP is not possible at all.
ff6e10c4a967.porting: PostgreSQL: LEFT/RIGHT/SUBSTRING/CONCAT/COALESCE/GREATEST/LEAST/LOWER/UPPER/TRIM/CAST are standard and port unchanged. IFNULL becomes COALESCE, IF(a,b,c) becomes CASE WHEN a THEN b ELSE c END, and CONCAT_WS exists but treats NULLs differently - those three need rewriting, the rest do not.

9e93e1c3f132.reason: An aggregate given an alias inside a SELECT list. Laravel's ->count()/->sum()/->avg()/->min()/->max() are first-class but each computes ONE value and issues its own statement; there is no builder form for 'select these aggregates, aliased, alongside these columns'. The only conversion available is ->select(DB::raw('COUNT(*) AS cnt')), and DB::raw is itself a raw site in this inventory - the site would move from surface fragment to surface expression and nothing would be converted. Splitting one grouped scan into N separate aggregate queries is not equivalent either. Recorded separately for the expression surface (DB::raw) because the extractor classifies the two differently, but the construct - and the reason it cannot leave SQL - is identical.
9e93e1c3f132.porting: PostgreSQL: standard SQL, ports unchanged. GROUP_CONCAT is the exception - it becomes string_agg(expr, delim) with a different argument order, and any ORDER BY inside it moves too.

Laravel's ->count()/->sum()/->avg()/->min()/->max() are first-class but each computes ONE value and issues its own statement; there is no builder form for 'select these aggregates, aliased, alongside these columns'. 8105334c0116.reason: MySQL spatial functions and the project's own haversine() SQL function. The builder has no spatial vocabulary at all, so these can only ever be raw text; converting means DB::raw, which converts nothing. They are also the statements most likely to be index-sensitive, so rewriting their shape casually risks a table scan on locations.
8105334c0116.porting: PostgreSQL/PostGIS: ST_Contains/ST_Intersects/ST_Within carry over by name, but SRID axis order differs (MySQL is lat/lng for 4326, PostGIS is lng/lat) and will silently transpose coordinates if unhandled. haversine() is a project-defined MySQL function with no Postgres counterpart - port it as ST_DWithin on geography, which is both correct and index-assisted, rather than translating the arithmetic.

Doing the work in PHP instead is not equivalent: LEFT(textbody, 500) truncates in the database so only 500 bytes cross the wire, and the queries using it are batch jobs over large text columns where that is the point. IFNULL becomes COALESCE, IF(a,b,c) becomes CASE WHEN a THEN b ELSE c END, and CONCAT_WS exists but treats NULLs differently - those three need rewriting, the rest do not.

810db37c95be.reason: Functions the DATABASE must evaluate: RAND() for sampling, and the clock/date arithmetic family (NOW, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, YEAR). The builder equivalents would compute the value in PHP and bind it, which moves the clock from the database to the application and changes what the query means under clock skew, timezone differences, or a long-running batch. DATEDIFF is the sharpest case: it counts CALENDAR DAY boundaries, so rewriting DATEDIFF(NOW(), t) < 2 as t >= now()->subDays(2) silently changes which rows match. These stay raw on correctness grounds, not convenience.
810db37c95be.porting: PostgreSQL: NOW() and CURRENT_DATE carry over; RAND() becomes random(); DATE_SUB/DATE_ADD become interval arithmetic (t - interval '1 day'); DATEDIFF has no direct equivalent and becomes a date subtraction yielding an integer, which is the same calendar-day semantics. Each needs rewriting, none needs redesigning.
